definition: In theoretical computer science and formal language theory, a tree transducer (TT) is an abstract machine taking as input a tree, and generating output – generally other trees, but models producing words or other structures exist.
details: Roughly speaking, tree transducers extend tree automata in the same way that word transducers extend word automata. Manipulating tree structures instead of words enable TT to model syntax-directed transformations of formal or natural languages. However, TT are not as well-behaved as their word counterparts in terms of algorithmic complexity, closure properties, etcetera. explainer.lead: A tree transducer is an abstract machine that takes a tree as input and generates output, generally other trees, though some models produce words or other structures. It matters because manipulating trees rather than words lets it model syntax-directed transformations of formal and natural languages.

tiers.eli5: It's a machine that eats a branching tree structure and spits out another one, like rewriting a sentence's grammar diagram.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use tree transducers to model syntax-directed transformations, but must account for the classes behaving less well than word counterparts.
tiers.paperLevel: Tree transducers extend tree automata as word transducers extend word automata; they are not as well-behaved as word counterparts in algorithmic complexity and closure properties, and most main classes are not closed under composition.

explainer.example: A transducer that takes a parsed sentence tree and outputs a transformed tree models a syntax-directed language transformation.
